title: Finite-Time Optomechanical Cooling by Multi-Exceptional-Point Braiding
abstract: Cooling protocols are usually optimized through static detunings and damping rates. Here we show that exceptional-point braiding can enhance finite-time optomechanical cooling under a fixed drive-power resource. We consider an auxiliary-cavity-assisted optomechanical system whose full three-mode drift contains two second-order exceptional points. Using the same prescribed power waveform for every protocol, we optimize only the detuning trajectory while matching its duration, endpoint, range, mean, and integrated control effort. Encircling either exceptional point produces a distinct pairwise eigenbranch exchange, whereas enclosing both generates a three-branch spectral cycle. The optimized two-EP trajectory lowers the final mechanical occupation by \(19.2\%\) relative to the optimized non-enclosing class and by \(9.9\%\) relative to the best single-EP protocol. A full Bogoliubov calculation including counter-rotating Stokes processes preserves this hierarchy. These results establish multi-exceptional-point braiding as a controllable resource for finite-time mechanical state preparation.
summary: The paper shows that by designing the time evolution path in the detuning-power plane to braid around two exceptional points, one can significantly enhance finite-time optomechanical cooling. This topological control method outperforms protocols based on single EPs or simple closed loops, establishing EP braiding as a powerful resource for quantum state engineering.
main_problem: The study demonstrates that controlling the system's evolution by braiding around multiple exceptional points (EPs) can significantly enhance finite-time cooling in an optomechanical setup.
main_result: Traversing a path that encloses two EPs yields the lowest final mechanical occupation, outperforming single-EP enclosures and non-enclosing paths by significant margins.
method: The authors optimize the detuning trajectory ($\Delta_M(t)$) while keeping the drive power fixed, comparing protocols based on their topological winding numbers around the EPs.
model_or_system: The system is an auxiliary-cavity-assisted optomechanical setup modeled by a full three-mode linearized Bogoliubov dynamics. The dynamics are governed by the evolution of the covariance matrix or the Bogoliubov vector, incorporating coupling between mechanical and optical modes.
key_observables:
Final mechanical occupation $n_m(T)$ (the primary cooling metric); topological winding numbers ($
u_D$) characterizing the control path.
important_parameters: Fixed drive power resource; detuning trajectory $\Delta_M(t)$; presence of two distinct exceptional points (EP1 and EP2).
main_assumptions: The comparison is made fair by matching shared resources like total duration, mean detuning, and integrated control effort across all topological classes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the optimized control-plane trajectories in the $(\Delta_M, P_L)$ plane for different winding numbers (C0, C1, C2, C12) and compare the resulting mechanical occupation $n_m(T)$ across these paths.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model, defines the control parameter space using EPs, optimizes detuning trajectories based on topological enclosure, and finally compares the resultant cooling performance (mechanical occupation) under both RWA and full Bogoliubov treatments.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of how geometric control in parameter space (topological invariants like EP braiding) can be leveraged as a controllable resource to achieve superior quantum state preparation compared to standard optimization techniques.
